title: Maitreyi's question
hook: offered her share of the property, Maitreyi asks the one question that makes the settlement worthless
tomorrow: "the self is to be seen, heard, reflected on"

segments.voice: Yesterday, sannyasa: Yajnavalkya was going forth to wander, and offered to settle his property first. Your line was a life moves in four stages.

Papers on the table. Everything divided, fair and square. Sign here. And instead of signing, Maitreyi asks a question. Sir, if this whole earth, full of wealth, belonged to me, would that make me immortal? Yajnavalkya is an honest man. No, he says. Your life would be like the life of the rich, but there's no hope of deathlessness through wealth. Then she says the line this day is named for.
screen: `SIGN HERE.` → `WOULD THE WHOLE EARTH MAKE ME IMMORTAL?` → `NO.`

segments.voice: What would I do with something that won't make me immortal? Tell me what you know. She doesn't refuse the money in a temper, and she doesn't make a speech about it. She sees that the settlement answers the wrong question, and asks for the right one. Notice the word she uses: amrita, deathless, the same word as the nectar the gods churned from the ocean. She wants the thing that doesn't end. Here's one of Hinduism's big maps of a life. Tradition later named four aims: dharma, doing right; artha, wealth and security; kama, love and pleasure; and moksha, freedom from the round of death and birth. Wealth is a real aim, not a sin. Maitreyi just sees it can't give the last one. And Yajnavalkya is delighted. You were always dear to me, he says, and now you say what's dear. Come, sit. I'll explain it to you, and as I do, reflect on it. His first words are strange. Truly, it is not for the husband's sake that a husband is dear. Not for the wife's sake that a wife is dear. Not for the sons' sake that sons are dear. Not for wealth's sake that wealth is dear. And on: not for the gods' sake are the gods dear, not for all beings' sake are all beings dear. Today, stay with the first half, the not. It isn't cold. Yajnavalkya is saying: look again. Something in the love isn't about them at all. Tomorrow, the second half of the sentence, the part that says what love is for.
screen: `WHAT WOULD I DO WITH IT?` · `AMRITA: THE DEATHLESS.` · `DHARMA, ARTHA, KAMA, MOKSHA.` · `NOT FOR THE HUSBAND'S SAKE.` · then, large: `WEALTH CAN'T BUY THE DEATHLESS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you're chasing right now: money, a title, a house, being liked. Don't scold yourself; it's probably a fine thing, so just ask it her question, quietly: will you make me deathless? Notice the honest answer, then ask what would, and let the question sit with you the way she sat down to listen.
Maitreyi. Offered her share of everything, she asks for amrita, the deathless, the one thing the whole earth full of wealth couldn't give her.
Your line: wealth can't buy the deathless. Tomorrow, a drum, a conch and a vina. Day three hundred sixty-seven, done.

screen: `DAY 367 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: "THE SELF IS TO BE SEEN, HEARD, REFLECTED ON."`

howItsDone: Maitreyi is remembered across Hindu tradition as a woman philosopher who chose knowledge over wealth; teachers of Vedanta often begin with her question when explaining why the Upanishads seek the self.

fork.setup: you're Maitreyi. your husband is leaving, and he offers you a fair share of everything he owns. what do you do?

ask whether all the wealth in the world would make you immortal.
fork.reveal: she asks, and he answers honestly: no. so she sets the money aside: what would I do with what won't make me deathless? tell me what you know.

original.note: Sanskrit amṛta: a (not) + mṛta (dead). deathless, and the nectar of immortality.

trapdoor: what you thought: a woman refusing alimony.
what it means: Maitreyi sees the settlement answers the wrong question, and asks for what doesn't end.
what a scholar hears: amṛta, not-dead, the same word as the gods' nectar. Yajnavalkya's answer opens with "not for the husband's sake is the husband dear" (2.4.5).

moksha.meaning: freedom from the round of death and birth; the last of the four aims

artha.meaning: wealth and security, one of the four aims of life

notes: Maitreyi's question and Yajnavalkya's reply (2.4.2–3) are paraphrased, not quoted; the outline title's English wording is kept as the index title.
'You were always dear to me, and now you say what's dear' paraphrases 2.4.4; confirm.
The list in 2.4.5 includes husband, wife, sons, wealth, Brahmins, Kshatriyas, worlds, gods, beings, all; the script names a selection. Confirm.
'Repeated for well over two thousand years': the Brihadaranyaka is usually dated to the first half of the first millennium BCE; confirm.
Amrita linked to the churning-of-the-ocean nectar: same word; confirm the tie is appropriate.
